questions.text: What should architects do if the cost estimate exceeds the client's construction budget?

options.text: Accept the overrun silently, hoping the client will not notice the discrepancy
Discuss options: reduce scope, adjust quality, defer phases, or increase budget; lead this discussion with QS support
Blame the client for insufficient budget, suggesting they should have anticipated higher costs
Proceed without addressing the issue, assuming the budget will adjust itself during construction

rationale.a: Negligent; unaddressed budget overruns lead to disputes and financial stress during construction.
rationale.c: Unprofessional; architects should work with clients to find solutions, not blame.
rationale.d: Reckless; unaddressed budget gaps cause construction delays and conflicts.
rationale.correct: When estimate exceeds budget, architects and QS should facilitate client discussion on options: scope reduction, quality adjustment, phase deferral, or budget increase.
rationale.takeaway: When estimate exceeds budget, lead a professional discussion with options—don't proceed silently or blame the client.

questions.text: When is it most effective to engage a quantity surveyor for value engineering?

options.text: Only after construction starts, when changes are more costly and less effective
During schematic phase when design changes have lowest cost impact
During construction documents phase to analyze and reduce costs, but with limited flexibility
Never; value engineering is not necessary, as initial estimates are always accurate

rationale.a: Too late; construction-phase changes are most expensive.
rationale.c: Too late; DD phase changes cost more than schematic changes.
rationale.d: False; value engineering saves clients significant cost by optimizing design elements.
rationale.correct: Value engineering is most effective during schematic phase when design changes are least costly; post-schematic changes are expensive to implement.
rationale.takeaway: Engage QS early during schematic design—cost advice then influences design; cost analysis after design is fixed has limited impact.

questions.text: What is a bill of quantities (BOQ)?

options.text: marketing document used to promote construction projects
detailed list itemizing all materials, labor, and equipment required for construction
Only a list of costs, excluding detailed specifications
Not used in the Philippines, as local practices differ

rationale.a: Confuses BOQ with promotional material; BOQ is a technical contract document.
rationale.c: Incomplete; BOQ lists quantities and sometimes unit prices, but the main purpose is ensuring complete, accurate specifications.
rationale.d: False; BOQ is used in Philippines, especially for government projects and large commercial work.
rationale.correct: A BOQ is a comprehensive list prepared by the QS itemizing all materials, labor, equipment, and services required, enabling contractors to bid accurately.
rationale.takeaway: BOQ = detailed material and labor list—allows contractors to bid on specific quantities rather than guess from drawings.

questions.text: What is the typical accuracy range of cost estimates during the schematic design phase?

options.text: ±50% or more, indicating a high level of uncertainty typical of early design stages
±15-25% accuracy (AACE Class 3); useful for budget approval but not construction bidding
±5% accuracy, which is generally not achievable at this stage due to limited design information
100% accurate, which is an unrealistic expectation for any phase of design

rationale.a: Too broad; ±50% or more applies to order-of-magnitude/conceptual (pre-schematic) per AACE Class 5.
rationale.c: Too optimistic; ±5% requires construction documents with complete specifications.
rationale.d: False; no estimate is 100% accurate—actual costs depend on market, labor, and contractor variables.
rationale.correct: Schematic estimates based on building massing and major systems achieve ±20% accuracy—useful for client budget approval but not for final construction cost control.
rationale.takeaway: Schematic estimates are ±20% accurate—use for budget approval; final estimates approach ±5% accuracy.

questions.text: What is the difference between a cost estimate and a construction budget?

options.text: They are identical, which is a common misconception
Cost estimate is the architect's projection; construction budget is the client's authorized spending limit, which may differ
Budget is always higher, which is not necessarily true
Only the budget matters, which oversimplifies the relationship between the two

rationale.a: False; they serve different purposes and are often different amounts.
rationale.c: Not always; if estimate exceeds budget, architect and client must discuss scope reduction or budget increase.
rationale.d: Incomplete; both matter—if estimate exceeds budget, they must discuss options.
rationale.correct: Cost estimate is the architect's professional prediction; budget is the client's authorized spending limit, which may be higher (contingency) or lower (triggering value engineering).
rationale.takeaway: Estimate ≠ budget—architect projects PHP 50M, client authorizes PHP 45M budget; discuss options to align.

options.text: Person who measures land only and prepares topographic surveys for site development planning purposes
professional specializing in cost estimation, cost control, and contract management for construction projects
Only a contractor role limited to on-site material takeoff and procurement scheduling activities
Quantity surveyors do not exist in the Philippines and are recognized only in Commonwealth countries

rationale.a: Confuses QS with surveyor; QS focuses on cost management, not land measurement.
rationale.c: Incomplete; while contractors use QS services, QS is an independent professional role not exclusive to contractors.
rationale.d: False; QS services are available in the Philippines for complex projects.
rationale.correct: A quantity surveyor (QS) specializes in cost estimation, detailed bills of quantities, cost control monitoring, value engineering analysis, and contract management.
rationale.takeaway: QS is a cost management specialist—prepares detailed BOQ, analyzes bids, monitors construction costs, and advises on value engineering.

questions.text: How can architects improve the reliability of cost estimates over time?

options.text: Cost estimation cannot be improved without significant changes in market conditions and technological advancements.
Maintain cost databases for their region and building types; track actual costs against estimates; use BIM for accurate quantity takeoff
Guess based on feelings and intuition, which is not a reliable method for professional practice.
Cost databases are not available, making it difficult to track historical data and trends.

rationale.a: False; cost estimation improves with systematic data collection and analysis.
rationale.d: False; cost databases from suppliers, regional construction cost indices, and historical projects are available.
rationale.correct: Architects improve estimates by maintaining regional cost databases, analyzing actual costs against estimates to identify trends, and using BIM to automate accurate quantity takeoff.
rationale.takeaway: Build cost databases for your region and project types—track estimates vs. actuals to improve future accuracy and identify market trends.

questions.text: What assumptions should architects clearly state in cost estimates to prevent misinterpretation?

options.text: No assumptions need to be stated, as the estimate should be self-explanatory and comprehensive
Build type, materials, systems, site conditions, scope inclusions/exclusions, basis of estimate (databases, quotes), and accuracy range
Only the total cost, as detailed breakdowns are unnecessary for initial estimates
Assumptions are confidential and should not be disclosed to maintain competitive advantage

rationale.a: Reckless; unstated assumptions lead to client disputes.
rationale.c: Insufficient; total cost alone tells the client nothing about scope, and they may misinterpret estimate applicability.
rationale.d: Misconception; clear assumptions are client communication, not confidential.
rationale.correct: Clear assumptions prevent disputes—state building type, material selections, systems (concrete vs. steel), site conditions, what's included/excluded, data sources, and accuracy (±20%).
rationale.takeaway: State assumptions clearly—'Conventional 4-story RC, standard finishes, mid-range MEP, ±20% accuracy'—prevents client misunderstanding.

questions.text: What is the typical accuracy range of cost estimates after construction documents are finalized?

options.text: ±50% accuracy, which is not typical for finalized documents
±30% accuracy, which is more common in earlier design phases
±10-20% accuracy, suitable for bidding with complete specifications (AACE Class 2)
No accuracy is possible, which is an exaggeration

rationale.b: Too broad; detailed specs achieve better than ±30%.
rationale.d: False; detailed specifications enable reliable cost estimation.
rationale.correct: Construction documents with complete specifications enable accurate takeoff of all materials, labor, and equipment; accuracy approaches ±5%.
rationale.takeaway: After construction documents are finalized, cost estimates approach ±5% accuracy—these are used for bid preparation.

questions.explanation: Too broad; ±50% is conceptual-phase accuracy. Too broad; detailed specs achieve better than ±30%. False; detailed specifications enable reliable cost estimation. Construction documents with complete specifications enable accurate takeoff of all materials, labor, and equipment; accuracy approaches ±5%. After construction documents are finalized, cost estimates approach ±5% accuracy—these are used for bid preparation.

questions.text: What should the architect's service agreement specify regarding cost estimation scope and accuracy?

options.text: No specification is needed, which is incorrect as cost estimation is crucial
Which phases include cost estimates, the accuracy range (±20% schematic, ±5% final), whether QS is engaged, and responsibilities for detailed takeoff
Only the final bid amount, which does not cover the full scope of cost estimation
Cost estimation is never mentioned in agreements, which is a misconception

rationale.a: Reckless; vague cost estimation responsibility creates disputes.
rationale.c: Insufficient; final bid is contractor-provided, not architect-provided estimate.
rationale.d: False; cost estimation scope must be clearly defined in service agreements.
rationale.correct: Service agreements must clarify cost estimation scope: which phases include estimates, accuracy ranges, QS engagement, detailed takeoff responsibility—preventing disputes.
rationale.takeaway: Service agreement must specify which design phases include cost estimates and their accuracy ranges to prevent client disputes.
